meta.title: AI-Assisted Decision-Making — Framework Data Snapshot
meta.source: Notion project 'AI Assisted Decision-Making' (3 linked databases)
meta.structure: factors (framework nodes) <- mechanisms (directional claims) <- studies (coded evidence). Mechanisms are the join: each names one factor and lists supporting and contradicting studies.
meta.id_scheme: Stable slugs assigned at export. 'notion_url' on every record is the canonical Notion page.
data_notes: STALE RELATIONS DROPPED. The 'Mechanisms' relation on Factors and the 'Supports/Contradicts mechanisms' relation on Studies both still point at ~24 DELETED mechanism pages from before the merge into the current 12 (verified: page 3b17da29e21381998d34ed2daf3fa899 returns deleted=true). Those pointers are excluded here. All factor-mechanism-study links in this file are derived from the 12 live Mechanisms rows, whose own relations are current and internally consistent.

34 of 35 studies link to at least one live mechanism. The exception is 's-timepressure-2024' — it has no mechanism links, no author, no DOI, and null summary/framing (its Design notes record that the row 'had been blanked at some point during the session'). Treat as incomplete.
One relation/notes mismatch: m-engagement-cost's Notes cite five merged sources including 'Time-pressure 2024', but the Supporting Studies relation holds four. The relation is used here.
Rollup fields 'N Support' and 'N Contradict' are not queryable via SQL; counts in this file are computed from the relation arrays.

components.label: Human
components.note: What the decision-maker brings. Largely fixed for a given deployment.

components.label: Task
components.note: What the decision is like. Inherited from the domain.

components.label: AI Ecosystem
components.note: What can actually be changed at design time. All three factors here are levers.

factors.definition: What the decision-maker already knows — about the task, about AI in general, and about this particular system. Largely fixed for a given deployment: in healthcare the decision-makers are clinicians, and you cannot change that.
factors.sub_factors: Task expertise · AI expertise / AI literacy · AI system usage (familiarity with this specific system over time)
factors.gap_note: Task expertise is well covered. AI literacy has one data point (Leichtmann: no effect). Longitudinal system usage has NONE — every study in the base is a first-encounter study, flagged in CAT §2.2.1.

factors.definition: The decision-maker's disposition to engage with cognitively demanding work. The personality trait most consistently measured in this literature, on the assumption that people who enjoy thinking will engage rather than defer.
factors.sub_factors: Need for Cognition (N4C) · Big Five traits · propensity to trust technology
factors.gap_note: CODING GAP, NOT AN EVIDENCE GAP. Three studies (Buçinca 2021, Gajos 2022, Contrastive-misconceptions 2025) measured NFC; the spreadsheet records THAT it was measured but not WHAT it did. Extract the directional findings and this factor becomes live.

factors.definition: Whether the decision is made by one person or several, and how they are structured. Almost the entire literature assumes a single decision-maker facing a single AI.
factors.sub_factors: Number of human decision-makers · leadership and hierarchy · group vs individual
factors.gap_note: One coded study (Chiang 2023). YOUR CHI 2025 paper is a second and would move this above the bar immediately. This is one of your four thesis contributions — the thinness here is the argument for it.

factors.definition: How hard the decision is: cognitive demand, complexity, and how uncertain the correct answer is. Determines how expensive it is for the human to work the problem independently rather than defer.
factors.sub_factors: Task complexity · cognitive demand · outcome uncertainty (prognostic vs diagnostic)
factors.gap_note: Difficulty itself is well covered. Outcome uncertainty rests on a single study and is absent from Fig. 2.1 — add it as a named sub-factor.

factors.definition: What it costs to be wrong. Raises the value of getting the decision right, and appears to lower how much people say they trust the AI — though not necessarily how much they actually defer to it.
factors.sub_factors: Risk / consequence of error · perceived personal exposure
factors.gap_note: All the evidence is on SELF-REPORTED trust. No study in the base tests whether higher stakes change behavioural reliance. That dissociation is worth a study of its own.

factors.definition: Whether the decision is made under time pressure or in a stress-inducing environment. Compresses the time available to verify, which is exactly the resource that catching a wrong AI requires.
factors.sub_factors: Time pressure · induced stress · interruption and workload
factors.gap_note: One coded study. Rastogi 2022 (Deciding Fast and Slow) is almost certainly a second but has never been coded — code it and this moves above the bar. Nothing at all on stress that is not time pressure.

factors.definition: How good the AI is — both in absolute terms and, more importantly, relative to the human it is advising. Complementary team performance depends on the second, not the first.
factors.sub_factors: Absolute accuracy / F1 · accuracy relative to the human · complementary expertise · information asymmetry
factors.gap_note: BIGGEST CODING GAP IN THE BASE. 24 of 35 studies report absolute accuracy but leave accuracy-relative-to-human unresolved, even though Bansal's central finding is about the relative quantity.

factors.definition: How the AI is presented and when — everything about the interaction other than the explanation itself. The most directly designable factor, and the one where the evidence most openly disagrees.
factors.sub_factors: Interaction protocol and timing (AI-first / human-first / on-demand / default) · confidence display · modality and embodiment (screen vs robot) · assertiveness of delivery · second opinions
factors.gap_note: Protocol is genuinely contested 2-2: Green and Buçinca favour human-first, Cabitza found AI-first produced HIGHER accuracy. Embodiment is an empty node — your IROS 2026 submission is the evidence. Confidence display may deserve promotion to its own factor: it calibrated reliance where explanations did not.

factors.definition: Whether the AI explains itself, and how. The most studied intervention in the field and the one with the most contradictory results — those contradictions largely resolve once you separate explanations that hand over a rationale from explanations that require the human to produce one.
factors.sub_factors: Presence vs absence · type and stance (substitutive vs generative) · cognitive load · quality
factors.gap_note: Densest node in the framework: 7 mechanisms. Explanation QUALITY rests on one study and is absent from Fig. 2.1 entirely. The substitutive/generative distinction is coded from summaries rather than source papers — re-code blind before publishing it.

mechanisms.claim: Explanations that withhold the conclusion and require the human to produce a judgement reduce over-reliance and build skill; explanations that hand over a rationale do not
mechanisms.notes: MERGED FROM: Gajos and Mamykina (CLEANEST EXPERIMENT IN THE BASE — three conditions, learning gains ONLY where the conclusion was withheld, identical explanatory content), Chen/Liao (within-study: feature-based increased over-reliance, example-based achieved complementarity), Cabitza pro-hoc ('Frictional AI'), Cabitza judicial (oracular to judicial), Ma (procedural deliberation), Buçinca 2021 (cognitive forcing), Buçinca 2025 (contrastive knowledge-gap alignment). TWO CAVEATS THAT MUST BE STATED: (1) GATED BY COGNITIVE LOAD — the two highest-load cases came out flat on over-reliance; (2) SEVERE LAB CONCENTRATION — four of seven are Gajos/Buçinca at Harvard, two are Cabitza/Natali. CONTRADICTION: Cabitza Rams found AI-first produced HIGHER diagnostic accuracy than human-first, with real radiologists on hard cases.

mechanisms.claim: A coherent-looking explanation substitutes for verification — people stop checking the recommendation because the explanation feels like understanding
mechanisms.notes: MERGED FROM: Cabitza 2024 Harmful (the 'XAI HALO EFFECT' — accurate advice plus misleading explanation, participants 'did not verify the correctness of the advice'), Bussone (fuller explanation raised trust AND produced over-reliance), Bansal 2021 ('explanations increased reliance on recommendations even when the AI was incorrect'), He 2025 conversational XAI (understanding and trust both rose while over-reliance was unchanged). THE MECHANISM IS FORM, NOT COST: harm arrives through the explanation looking right, independent of how much effort it demands. Sharpest evidence that an explanation can satisfy a transparency requirement while degrading oversight. CONTRADICTION: Leichtmann found attribution plus example-based explanations improved outcomes and produced better-calibrated trust.

mechanisms.claim: Reliance is not one quantity — over-reliance, under-reliance and subjective trust move independently, so an intervention can improve one and leave the failure mode untouched
mechanisms.notes: STRUCTURAL / MEASUREMENT MECHANISM — it constrains how every other row in this table may be read. MERGED FROM: Schemmer (explanations moved RAIR significantly, RSR not at all — uptake of good advice improved, resistance to bad advice did not), Sivaraman (expert reliance is partial and component-wise — 'ignore, trust, or NEGOTIATE' — so binary agreement measures are mis-specified), Buçinca 2020 (proxy tasks do not generalise to real decision tasks and subjective measures do not predict objective performance), He 2025 (understanding and trust rose while over-reliance held constant), Salimzadeh (reliance moved with uncertainty while trust did not move at all). FIVE STUDIES, FOUR INDEPENDENT GROUPS. Practical rule: any mechanism in this table whose only evidence is trust or preference is on weaker ground than one evidenced behaviourally.

mechanisms.claim: Explanation effects on decision quality are not main effects — they are moderated by AI performance, risk and task, and are frequently null or negative
mechanisms.notes: MERGED FROM: Alufaisan (three-arm design with a no-AI control — 'the why information provided in explainable AI may not enhance user decision-making'), de Brito Duarte (OWN MSc — explanation effect on trust is jointly conditional on system performance and risk level), Wang and Yin (four XAI methods on two task types — most 'not as helpful as expected and even harmful at times'). CONTESTED BY DESIGN: Vasconcelos and Gajos both produce clear positive effects under specified conditions. The right reading is not that explanations do nothing but that the unconditional question 'do explanations help?' is malformed — which is itself the argument for a factor-conditioned framework.

mechanisms.claim: Calibrated reliance depends on the human holding an accurate mental model of WHEN the AI fails — which case-level confidence supports and explanations do not
mechanisms.notes: MERGED FROM: Bansal 2019a (error boundary mediates AI accuracy to team performance), Bansal 2019b (updates that improve the model HURT the team by invalidating the learned failure pattern), Zhang 2020 (case-level confidence calibrates, global accuracy cannot), Bansal 2021 (users built mental models from confidence and used it whether or not explanations were shown), Reverberi (experts weight-integrate: OR 3.48 correct vs 1.85 incorrect, with NO explanation), Kiani (model performance in isolation does not transfer; benefit confined to an experience band), Leichtmann (case-level explanation helped, general education about the AI did not). LARGEST AND MOST INDEPENDENT SUPPORT SET IN THE BASE. CONTRADICTION: Bussone found system confidence had only a slight effect — with domain experts, where the mental model may already exist.

mechanisms.claim: Advice the decision-maker requested behaves differently from advice imposed on them — control over the information flow, not the information, determines the reliance profile
mechanisms.notes: MERGED FROM: Lu, Wang and Yin (three pre-registered experiments — ALWAYS-PRESENT second opinions cut over-reliance but RAISED under-reliance, regardless of whether the source was a peer or another AI; SOLICITED second opinions mitigated over-reliance WITHOUT that penalty), Westphal (decision control — empowering users to ADJUST recommendations — raised trust, understanding and compliance, while explanation presence in the same study did the opposite). THE CONTENT IS HELD CONSTANT IN BOTH: what changes is who decides when it arrives and whether it can be altered. Directly relevant to RQ6: a multi-agent setting is by construction the always-present condition, which this mechanism predicts will trade over-reliance for under-reliance.

mechanisms.claim: How the AI speaks changes how much it is believed — identical content in a different register produces different reliance
mechanisms.notes: MERGED FROM: Calisto (assertive versus suggestive tone delivering IDENTICAL breast-cancer diagnostic content; personalising assertiveness to clinician experience REDUCED MEDICAL ERRORS and raised satisfaction), Zhang, Lee and Carter ('embracing' language INCREASED reliance, 'distancing' language REDUCED it — same information, differently worded). TWO INDEPENDENT STUDIES, DIFFERENT POPULATIONS (clinicians and crowdworkers), SAME CONCLUSION. Mechanism is social and communicative rather than cognitive: nothing about the information changes, only the register in which it is asserted, and the optimal register depends on the recipient's expertise. The most under-theorised family in the literature.

mechanisms.claim: Forcing an independent judgement before showing the AI can backfire, entrenching a wrong prior or triggering rejection of correct advice
mechanisms.notes: FROM: Cabitza Rams — AI-FIRST protocols were associated with HIGHER diagnostic accuracy than human-first, with 12 specialist radiologists on knee MRI and 44 ECG readers. The authors name the mechanisms: ALGORITHMIC AVERSION (seeing the AI first can trigger rejection of correct advice) and CONSERVATISM BIAS (committing first can entrench a wrong prior). THIS IS THE DIRECT COUNTERWEIGHT to the withheld-conclusion mechanism, and it is the only study in the base run with real domain experts on genuinely hard clinical cases. Below bar on one study, but it is a high-quality one and the disagreement is real rather than a coding artefact — do not resolve it prematurely.

mechanisms.claim: People engage with an explanation only when engaging is cheaper than the cost of being wrong — so difficulty, time and explanation load determine over-reliance
mechanisms.notes: MERGED FROM: Vasconcelos (cost-benefit framework, 5 studies N=731, manipulates both cost and benefit), Westphal (only MEASURED mediator in the base — explanation harm ran through increased perceived task complexity), Rastogi (time as the scarce resource), Time-pressure 2024 (pressure raises over-reliance while holding accuracy), Buçinca 2021 (people default to heuristics rather than per-case analysis because analysis is costly). FOUR INDEPENDENT LABS converging from three theories. CONTRADICTION: Green and Chen varied presentation across six conditions — effectively varying cost — and reliance still did not track performance, suggesting cost is not the whole story.

mechanisms.claim: When the task makes verification impossible rather than merely expensive, reliance rises and no amount of explanation design fixes it
mechanisms.notes: MERGED FROM: Salimzadeh ('individuals may lack sufficient capability to verify the correctness of AI advice' under uncertainty), Green and Chen (participants could evaluate neither their own nor the model's accuracy across all six treatments — the 'empty cycle of oversight'), Wang and Yin (explanations convey reasoning but not model uncertainty, leaving no basis for selective override). CRITICALLY DISTINCT FROM THE COST MECHANISM: lowering the price of checking does nothing when checking is not possible. This is the strongest argument in the base against assuming EU AI Act Article 14 human oversight is protective in prognostic or high-uncertainty deployments.

mechanisms.claim: Acceptance of AI advice is path-dependent — it accumulates across a sequence of encounters rather than being decided afresh each time
mechanisms.notes: FROM: Wang, Lu and Yin (WWW 2022 Best Paper) — models human acceptance across a SEQUENCE of binary trials using the AI's recommendation and confidence as inputs. The contribution is predictive rather than explanatory, but the structural claim matters: acceptance is treated as accumulating over trials, not as an independent per-case decision. THE ONLY PLACE IN THIS ENTIRE BASE WHERE THE LONGITUDINAL DIMENSION IS TOUCHED, alongside Bansal 2019b on model updates. Every other study is a first encounter with a static system — which is exactly the gap flagged in CAT section 2.2.1 and a live opening for the thesis.

mechanisms.claim: Group deliberation raises reliance on the AI overall while concentrating scrutiny on fewer cases
mechanisms.notes: FROM: Chiang (groups relied on the AI MORE than individuals regardless of correctness, but were MORE CONFIDENT when they did overturn incorrect recommendations, and made fairer decisions on an accuracy-equality criterion; decision accuracy itself did not differ). The group is not a neutral container for AI advice — deliberation appears to redistribute where scrutiny lands rather than increase how much there is. BELOW BAR ON ONE STUDY ONLY. Regina's CHI 2025 paper (The Amplifying Effect of Explainability in Groups) is the second study and would move this above the bar immediately — add it to the evidence base.

studies.study: The Role of Explanations on Trust and Reliance in Clinical Decision Support Systems
studies.author: Bussone, Stumpf, O'Sullivan
studies.summary_of_findings: The earliest study in this base to name BOTH failure modes at once, and it names them as a trade-off. A FULLER explanation of the facts used in making a diagnosis had a positive effect on trust but ALSO led to over-reliance. LESS detailed explanations made participants question the system's reliability and led to SELF-RELIANCE problems (under-reliance). System confidence had only a SLIGHT effect on trust and reliance. Participants wanted better explanations in order to interpret the system's confidence, verify the disorder fit the suggestion, understand the reasoning chain, and make differential diagnoses.
studies.authors_framing: AUTHORS' FRAMING: explanation detail is a CALIBRATION DIAL with failure at both ends — too much detail produces inappropriate over-reliance, too little produces dismissal of valid recommendations. This is a DOSAGE mechanism, distinct from the type, quality and cost accounts elsewhere in the base. IMPORTANT TENSION: the finding that confidence had only a slight effect directly contradicts Zhang 2020 and Bansal 2021, where confidence carried the calibration work. Bussone's participants were domain experts and theirs were lay users — that difference is the obvious candidate explanation and is worth testing.
studies.design_notes: EXPLANATION DETAIL: fuller versus less detailed explanations of the facts used to reach a diagnosis, inside a CDSS prototype. System CONFIDENCE was also displayed. Exploratory user study in which healthcare professionals diagnosed hypothetical cases involving patients with a balance-related disorder.

studies.study: Beyond Accuracy: The Role of Mental Models in Human-AI Team Performance
studies.author: Bansal, Nushi, Kamar, Lasecki, Weld, Horvitz
studies.summary_of_findings: Establishes the claim that most of this literature then assumes: achieving high team performance depends on MORE THAN THE ACCURACY of the AI system. Because the human and the AI may have different expertise, the highest team performance is reached when both know how and when to complement one another. Awareness of the AI's error boundary is what lets the human decide when to accept and when to override. This is the foundational statement of the complementarity argument that Bansal 2021 and You Complete Me 2022 later test directly.
studies.authors_framing: AUTHORS' FRAMING: the human's MENTAL MODEL OF THE AI'S ERROR BOUNDARY is the mediating variable between AI accuracy and team performance. If the error boundary is learnable, the human can develop an accurate mental model and override selectively; if it is not, accuracy gains do not transfer to the team. Mechanism is knowledge-about-the-model rather than knowledge-about-the-case — which distinguishes it from Zhang 2020's case-level confidence account, and the two are worth reading against each other.
studies.design_notes: Properties of the AI's ERROR BOUNDARY — the structure of where the model fails — rather than any explanation or interface feature. The object of study is the human's MENTAL MODEL of the AI's capabilities, specifically their answer to 'When does the AI err?'. CATEGORY CAVEAT: what was varied is the STRUCTURE of the error boundary (how learnable or parsimonious it is), not simply the accuracy level. 'AI performance: High / Low' is the closest available category and understates the manipulation — consider adding an 'AI performance: Error boundary structure' category.

studies.study: Updates in Human-AI Teams: Understanding and Addressing the Performance/Compatibility Tradeoff
studies.author: Bansal, Nushi, Kamar, Weld, Lasecki, Horvitz
studies.summary_of_findings: THE ONE LONGITUDINAL RESULT IN THE BASE, and a counterintuitive one: UPDATES THAT INCREASE AI PERFORMANCE MAY HURT TEAM PERFORMANCE. A successful partnership requires the human to develop insight into the AI's failures; an update changes the failure pattern, invalidating the mental model the user built, at odds with their prior experience and confidence. Empirically, current machine learning algorithms do NOT produce compatible updates. The proposed re-training objective recovers the tradeoff, enabling updates that are both more compatible and accurate.
studies.authors_framing: AUTHORS' FRAMING: the mechanism is INVALIDATION OF THE USER'S MENTAL MODEL. Reliance is built on accumulated experience of when the AI fails; an update rewrites that failure pattern without warning, so previously calibrated reliance becomes miscalibrated even though the model got better. Directly fills the 'AI system usage over time' gap flagged as empty in CAT section 2.2.1 — and it says the gap matters, because the entire rest of this base studies first encounters with a static model.
studies.design_notes: MODEL UPDATES OVER TIME — the only study in this base that varies the AI across a user's experience of it rather than holding it fixed. Introduces the notion of COMPATIBILITY of an AI update with prior user experience, and evaluates it empirically on three high-stakes classification tasks. Also proposes a re-training objective that penalises NEW errors in order to trade performance against compatibility.

studies.study: The Principles and Limits of Algorithm-in-the-Loop Decision Making
studies.author: Green, Chen
studies.summary_of_findings: Presenting the risk assessment DID increase accuracy in almost every case — but participants' decisions were both UNRELIABLE and RACIALLY BIASED. Across both settings and all six treatments, participants were unable to consistently evaluate the quality of their own or the risk assessment's predictions. In all but one case, participants did NOT differentiate their reliance on the risk assessment according to how it actually performed — they did not adjust strategy to the details of each case. 'Disparate interactions' were present across all settings and treatments: in the companion study, the risk assessment exerted 25.9% stronger influence toward HIGHER risk predictions for black than white defendants.
studies.authors_framing: AUTHORS' FRAMING, and the single most quotable line in this base for the Article 14 argument: 'the adoption of machine learning decision making aids will create an EMPTY CYCLE OF OVERSIGHT. Algorithms are implemented to improve human decision making, then those same humans are asked to oversee the algorithm's decisions. Yet our experiments suggest that people are unable to provide the types of oversight that are required.' Mechanism is a CAPABILITY failure rather than a motivational one — people cannot evaluate their own or the model's accuracy, so reliance cannot track performance no matter how it is presented. Six presentation conditions did not fix it.
studies.design_notes: SIX CONDITIONS for presenting the risk assessment, crossed with TWO SETTINGS: pretrial release and financial lending. Mechanical Turk participants saw narrative profiles of criminal defendants or loan applicants and predicted future outcomes (failure to appear, re-arrest, loan default); some also saw a machine-learning risk assessment trained on US Department of Justice and lending-company data. Participants were FINANCIALLY INCENTIVISED to report true predictions. After predicting, they reported beliefs about their OWN performance and the risk assessment's. Evaluated against three stated normative principles: accuracy, reliability, fairness. PROVENANCE NOTE: the CSCW page and publisher abstract are JavaScript-blocked; findings taken from Green and Chen's own AAAI-20 summary paper, which reports this study (cited there as Green and Chen 2019b). Verify against the CSCW PDF before quoting numbers.

studies.study: Proxy Tasks and Subjective Measures Can Be Misleading in Evaluating XAI Systems
studies.author: Buçinca, Lin, Gajos, Glassman
studies.summary_of_findings: Argues that XAI systems 'are rarely evaluated by measuring the performance of human+AI teams on actual decision-making tasks', and shows why that matters: results from proxy tasks do NOT generalise to real decision tasks, and subjective measures do NOT predict objective performance. This is a validity warning that applies to a large share of the rest of this evidence base — any row here whose only outcomes are trust or preference should be read in its light.
studies.authors_framing: NO SUBSTANTIVE MECHANISM PROPOSED — this is a measurement-validity paper. Its contribution to the framework is a constraint on admissible evidence rather than a claim about behaviour: subjective and proxy measures are not substitutes for behavioural outcomes. Pairs with Sivaraman 2023 (binary reliance measures mis-specified for expert decisions) as the two measurement critiques in the base. Together they argue that a good share of published XAI findings may be measuring the wrong thing.
studies.design_notes: METHODOLOGICAL STUDY rather than a factor study. Two online experiments plus one in-person think-aloud. Evaluates two common ways of assessing XAI systems: (1) PROXY TASKS, such as how well humans can predict the AI's decision from the explanation, and (2) SUBJECTIVE MEASURES of trust and preference used as predictors of actual performance.

studies.study: Impact of a deep learning assistant on the histopathologic classification of liver cancer
studies.author: Kiani, Uyumazturk, Rajpurkar et al.
studies.summary_of_findings: CORRECTS THE OLD CODING. Use of the assistant did NOT change the mean accuracy of the 11 pathologists (p=0.184, OR=1.281). It significantly improved accuracy (p=0.045, OR=1.499) only for the SUBSET OF NINE pathologists who fell within well-defined experience levels. The overall effect was null. The previous spreadsheet entry claimed assistance 'significantly improved diagnostic accuracy regardless of particular experience level or case difficulty level' — that reverses the headline result. This row is a concrete example of why the re-read was necessary.
studies.authors_framing: AUTHORS' FRAMING is descriptive rather than mechanistic. Their premise: although AI algorithms rival human performance on clinical tasks, 'their actual impact on human diagnosticians when incorporated into clinical workflows remains relatively unexplored.' The contribution is the workflow-integration finding — a model that performs well in isolation does not automatically transfer that performance to the assisted human, and the benefit that does emerge is confined to a defined experience band rather than distributed across all users.
studies.design_notes: PRESENCE OF AI ASSISTANCE, with EXPERTISE as the analysed moderator. 11 pathologists of varying experience classified hepatocellular carcinoma versus cholangiocarcinoma on H&E whole-slide images, with and without a deep-learning assistant. Model accuracy 0.885 on a 26-slide validation set and 0.842 on an 80-slide independent test set — coded Medium on the independent test figure, which is the honest one.

studies.study: Effect of confidence and explanation on accuracy and trust calibration in AI-assisted decision making
studies.author: Zhang, Liao, Bellamy
studies.summary_of_findings: Central distinction: showing a high overall accuracy figure can raise trust in and acceptance of a system, but does NOT help people tell apart the cases they can trust from the cases they should not. Confidence scores DID help calibrate trust case by case. But trust calibration alone was not sufficient to improve AI-assisted decision making — that also depends on whether the human brings enough unique knowledge to complement the AI's errors. Local feature-importance explanations did not deliver the calibration benefit that confidence did. Read together with Bansal 2021, which independently found participants built mental models from confidence and used it whether or not explanations were shown.
studies.authors_framing: AUTHORS' WORDS: what matters is 'appropriately calibrating human trust in the AI on a case-by-case basis,' because 'knowing when to trust or distrust the AI allows the human expert to appropriately apply their knowledge, improving decision outcomes in cases where the model is likely to perform poorly.' TWO-STEP MECHANISM: confidence enables case-level calibration; calibration only converts into better decisions if the human has complementary knowledge to contribute. Global accuracy figures cannot support case-level discrimination at all. This is the strongest argument in the base for treating confidence display as a channel distinct from explanation.
studies.design_notes: Two AI-design elements varied: display of the AI's CONFIDENCE SCORE, and display of a LOCAL EXPLANATION (feature importance for the specific case). Income prediction task. The conceptual move is to separate GLOBAL performance indicators (overall stated accuracy) from CASE-BY-CASE signals — the two do different work.

studies.study: Does Explainable AI Improve Human Decision-Making?
studies.author: Alufaisan, Marusich, Bakdash, Zhou, Kantarcioglu
studies.summary_of_findings: Objective decision accuracy compared across control, AI-only, and AI-plus-explanation. The result: 'the why information provided in explainable AI may not enhance user decision-making', at least in some situations. The authors are explicit that the literature is MIXED on whether XAI improves actual decision-making or the ability to spot model errors, and position their contribution as a clean objective-accuracy test rather than a subjective one.
studies.authors_framing: AUTHORS' FRAMING: the premise under test is that explanation 'offers potential for users to better understand and trust a model, and to recognize and correct AI predictions that are incorrect.' They report that premise not borne out for objective accuracy. NO POSITIVE MECHANISM IS PROPOSED — this is a null-result paper closing with 'further research may be needed to understand how to integrate explainable AI into real systems.' Use as a boundary case, not a mechanism source.
studies.design_notes: THREE-ARM COMPARISON on real datasets: objective human decision accuracy WITHOUT AI (control), WITH an AI prediction and no explanation, and WITH AI prediction plus explanation. The three-arm structure is what makes this useful — it separates the contribution of the recommendation from the contribution of the explanation. Most studies in this base omit the no-AI control entirely.

studies.study: Does the whole exceed its parts? Effect of AI Explanations on Complementary Team Performance
studies.author: Bansal, Wu, Zhou, Fok, Nushi, Kamar, Ribeiro, Weld
studies.summary_of_findings: N=1626 across three tasks (beer reviews, book reviews, LSAT logical reasoning). Complementary team performance was observed on EVERY task — but explanations offered no benefit over simply displaying the AI's confidence. Explanations increased reliance on recommendations even when the AI was incorrect. Explaining only the predicted class (Explain-Top-1) outperformed explaining the top two classes. Adaptive explanations (withheld when AI confidence fell below a threshold) successfully reduced blind agreement on low-confidence, more-likely-wrong cases. Over 70% of participants reported partially weighing the AI rather than following or ignoring it wholesale. AI accuracy was fixed at 84% (65% for LSAT, vs 67% human) so participants could not earn the bonus by blindly following the AI.
studies.authors_framing: AUTHORS' WORDS: 'explanations did not appear to offer benefit compared to simply displaying the AI's confidence. Notably, explanations increased reliance on recommendations even when the AI was incorrect.' They attribute the effect to confidence rather than explanation content: the AI's confidence is 'a simple, yet salient feature via which users create a mental model of the AI's global behavior.' Participants reported using confidence scores at the same rate whether or not explanations were shown. They also note that 'difference in expertise between human and AI affects whether (or how much) AI assistance will help achieve complementary performance.'
studies.design_notes: XAI: explanation presence and type — Explain-Top-1 (predicted class only), Explain-Top-2 (both classes), Adaptive (explanation withheld below a confidence threshold), and expert-generated explanations — against a confidence-only team baseline and a human-only baseline. AI confidence was DISPLAYED IN ALL team conditions, so the comparison isolates explanation over and above confidence. Three tasks spanning easy to hard (beer reviews, Amazon book reviews, LSAT logical reasoning); AI accuracy fixed at 84% for sentiment and 65% on LSAT against 67% human accuracy.

studies.study: To Trust or to Think: Cognitive Forcing Functions Can Reduce Overreliance on AI
studies.author: Buçinca, Malaya, Gajos
studies.summary_of_findings: N=199, nutrition task. Three cognitive forcing designs compared against two simple explainable-AI approaches and a no-AI baseline. Cognitive forcing SIGNIFICANTLY reduced over-reliance relative to the simple XAI approaches. But there is a trade-off the field tends to skip: participants gave the LEAST favourable subjective ratings to exactly the designs that reduced over-reliance most. The authors also ran an equity audit for intervention-generated inequality and found cognitive forcing benefited participants HIGHER in Need for Cognition more — so the intervention helps least the people most likely to defer. NOTE: Need for Cognition was measured as an individual-difference moderator, not manipulated.
studies.authors_framing: AUTHORS' WORDS: 'Informed by the dual-process theory of cognition, we posit that people rarely engage analytically with each individual AI recommendation and explanation, and instead develop general heuristics about whether and when to follow the AI suggestions.' The intervention works by compelling engagement rather than inviting it. Their concluding claim: 'human cognitive motivation moderates the effectiveness of explainable AI solutions.'
studies.design_notes: AI DESIGN is the manipulation: three cognitive forcing interventions (AI recommendation on demand; commit to your own answer before seeing the AI; slow down / enforced wait) compared against two simple explainable-AI conditions and a no-AI baseline. N=199, nutrition task, simulated AI at 75%. NEED FOR COGNITION was measured as an individual-difference covariate, not manipulated — it enters as a moderator in an equity audit for intervention-generated inequality.

studies.study: Are Explanations Helpful? A Comparative Study of the Effects of Explanations in AI-Assisted Decision-Making
studies.author: Wang, Yin
studies.summary_of_findings: Most XAI methods were NOT as helpful as expected, and were EVEN HARMFUL AT TIMES — for instance by causing over-reliance. Evidence remained inconclusive on whether they improve user accuracy or reduce over-reliance. The value of the paper is the direct comparison under one protocol: rather than one method against no-explanation, four methods against each other on two task types, evaluated against explicit criteria. Notably the middle criterion — helping people recognise MODEL UNCERTAINTY — is one almost no other study in this base evaluates at all.
studies.authors_framing: AUTHORS' FRAMING is diagnostic rather than mechanistic: they specify what a good explanation should DO (build understanding, expose uncertainty, calibrate trust) and show that common methods largely fail those tests. The implied mechanism is that explanations which convey the model's REASONING without conveying its UNCERTAINTY give users no basis for selective override — which converges with Zhang 2020 (confidence calibrates where feature importance does not) and with Bansal 2019 (the error boundary is the thing worth knowing).
studies.design_notes: FOUR established model-agnostic XAI METHODS compared head to head, crossed with TWO TYPES OF DECISION TASK, in randomised controlled experiments. The evaluation is structured around three properties the authors argue ideal explanations should satisfy: improve people's understanding of the model, help people recognise MODEL UNCERTAINTY, and support CALIBRATED trust. The middle criterion is one almost no other study in this base evaluates.

studies.study: Do People Engage Cognitively with AI? Impact of AI Assistance on Incidental Learning
studies.author: Gajos, Mamykina
studies.summary_of_findings: THE SHARPEST RESULT IN THE BASE ON EXPLANATION FORM. Participants had significant LEARNING GAINS from collaborating with the AI ONLY in the condition where they had to arrive at a conclusion themselves using the AI's explanations — compared with conditions where a conclusion, or both conclusion and explanation, were provided. Handing over the answer removed the learning even though identical explanatory content was present. Learning here is incidental learning, measured separately from in-the-moment decision accuracy.
studies.authors_framing: AUTHORS' WORDS: 'such incidental learning can only occur when people cognitively engage with the information they receive and process this information thoughtfully.' The mechanism is that WITHHOLDING THE CONCLUSION forces the processing that produces learning, while supplying the conclusion short-circuits it regardless of how good the explanation is. This is the closest thing in the base to direct experimental evidence that what matters is whether an explanation DELIVERS or DEMANDS a judgement — and it comes from the authors' own three-condition design, not from any reinterpretation.
studies.design_notes: THREE EXPERIMENTS on nutritional decisions with simulated AI recommendations and explanations. The critical manipulation is WHAT THE AI HANDS OVER: (a) a conclusion, (b) a conclusion PLUS explanation, or (c) explanations only, requiring the participant to arrive at the conclusion themselves. CAUTION: earlier coding recorded Need for Cognition as measured here; that is not verified in the portion read, so it is coded Not measured.

studies.study: Deciding Fast and Slow: The Role of Cognitive Biases in AI-assisted Decision-making
studies.author: Rastogi, Zhang, Wei, Varshney, Dhurandhar, Tomsett
studies.summary_of_findings: UPGRADED FROM PARTIAL — now read from the full abstract. Experiment 1 validates that a time-based de-anchoring strategy works in human-AI collaborative decision-making. Experiment 2 shows the sharper, conditional result: the time allocation strategy WITH EXPLANATION effectively de-anchors the human and improves collaborative performance SPECIFICALLY WHEN THE AI MODEL HAS LOW CONFIDENCE AND IS INCORRECT. That is precisely the case that matters — the intervention targets the cases where deference is most costly, rather than reducing reliance uniformly. The contribution includes a mathematical model of cognitive biases, not only an empirical test.
studies.authors_framing: AUTHORS' WORDS: people's 'perception and understanding are often distorted by their cognitive biases, such as confirmation bias, anchoring bias, availability bias'. They 'use knowledge from the field of cognitive science to account for cognitive biases in the human-AI collaborative decision-making setting, and mitigate their negative effects'. MECHANISM IS ANCHORING: the AI prediction functions as an anchor, and TIME is the resource that lets independent reasoning compete with it. Distinctive in this base for being formally modelled rather than only described, and for targeting the intervention at low-confidence cases rather than applying it uniformly.
studies.design_notes: TIME ALLOCATION as a designed resource, plus AI CONFIDENCE. Two user experiments. Experiment 1 implements a TIME-BASED DE-ANCHORING strategy and validates its effectiveness. Experiment 2 tests a time allocation strategy designed for a RESOURCE-CONSTRAINED setting — total time is finite, so time must be spent where it pays. The paper first mathematically models cognitive biases and offers a general framework for the interplay between cognitive biases and human-AI accuracy, then focuses on anchoring specifically.

studies.study: Experimental evidence of effective human-AI collaboration in medical decision-making
studies.author: Reverberi, Rigon, Solari, Hassan, Cherubini et al. (GI Genius CADx Study Group)
studies.summary_of_findings: The cleanest demonstration in this base of well-calibrated EXPERT reliance without any explanation. Endoscopists were influenced by the AI (OR=3.05) but not erratically: they followed AI advice more when it was CORRECT (OR=3.48) than when it was INCORRECT (OR=1.85). The differential is the finding — influence is real but discriminating. The authors characterise this as a weighted integration of the clinician's own opinion with the AI's, with reliance adjusted to the reliability of both sources. Calibration here came from domain expertise and real clinical material, not from XAI.
studies.authors_framing: AUTHORS' FRAMING: effective collaboration arises from 'a weighted integration of their own and the AI's opinions', with clinicians adjusting reliance according to the accuracy of both sources rather than accepting or rejecting wholesale. The paired odds ratios (3.48 when correct vs 1.85 when incorrect) are the evidence. NOTE the authors' own caveat that 'limited evidence-based knowledge exists about the context, design, and psychological mechanisms that craft optimal human-AI collaboration' — they demonstrate the outcome without isolating a psychological mechanism.
studies.design_notes: AI SUPPORT PRESENCE, within-subject: 21 endoscopists gave an optical diagnosis on 504 prospectively acquired colonoscopy lesion videos, both with and without AI assistance. EXPERTISE also varies and is analysed: 10 experts (at least 5 years of colonoscopy plus optical biopsy experience with virtual chromoendoscopy) versus 11 non-experts (fewer than 500 colonoscopies). Multicentric. No explanation of any kind was provided — which is what makes the calibrated-reliance result so striking.

studies.study: Will You Accept the AI Recommendation? Predicting Human Behavior in AI-Assisted Decision Making
studies.author: Wang, Lu, Yin
studies.summary_of_findings: Develops and evaluates a model predicting human acceptance of AI recommendations across a sequence of trials, using the AI's recommendation and confidence as inputs. The contribution is PREDICTIVE rather than explanatory — it forecasts acceptance behaviour rather than explaining why acceptance occurs. Best Paper Award at WWW 2022.
studies.authors_framing: NO PSYCHOLOGICAL MECHANISM PROPOSED. The contribution is a behavioural model of acceptance over sequential trials, not an account of why acceptance happens. Its value to the framework is structural: acceptance is treated as PATH-DEPENDENT across a sequence of trials, which is the only place in this entire base where the longitudinal dimension is touched at all. Worth following up precisely because 'AI system usage over time' is otherwise an empty node.
studies.design_notes: Not a factor-manipulation study — a MODELLING study. Participants solved a sequence of binary decision trials with AI assistance; on each trial the AI gave a binary recommendation plus its CONFIDENCE. The goal is to predict acceptance. NO FACTOR IS MANIPULATED, so 'Manipulated factors' is correctly empty here — the only row in the base where that is true by design rather than by gap. CAUTION: earlier coding attributed a 'risk of the task' manipulation to this paper; not verified, so stakes and difficulty remain Not reported.

studies.study: You Complete Me: Human-AI Teams and Complementary Expertise
studies.author: Zhang, Lee, Carter
studies.summary_of_findings: Two findings. First, on expertise: participants could PERCEIVE when the assistant was expert or non-expert within the same task and calibrated their reliance accordingly to improve team performance; as complementary expertise increased, participants identified the object correctly more often. Second, and newly recovered here: communicating expertise through the LINGUISTIC PROPERTIES of the explanation text was effective — EMBRACING language INCREASED reliance and DISTANCING language REDUCED it. The same information, differently worded, moved behaviour.
studies.authors_framing: AUTHORS' FRAMING: reliance tracks PERCEIVED relative expertise, and perceived expertise can be conveyed either by actual performance or by the WORDING of the explanation. Two routes to the same behavioural outcome. CONVERGENCE WORTH NOTING: this is the second study in the base showing that delivery register moves reliance independently of content — Calisto 2023 found the same for assertive versus suggestive tone with clinicians. Two independent studies, different populations, same conclusion: how the AI speaks is a live design lever, not packaging.
studies.design_notes: TWO manipulations. (1) RELATIVE EXPERTISE: the AI assistant's expertise relative to the participant, varied along a continuum from COMPLETELY OVERLAPPING to PERFECTLY COMPLEMENTARY. (2) LINGUISTIC PROPERTIES OF THE EXPLANATION TEXT: 'embracing' versus 'distancing' language used to communicate the assistant's expertise. Series of controlled online lab studies, object-identification task.

studies.study: Rams, hounds and white boxes: human-AI collaboration protocols in medical diagnosis
studies.author: Cabitza, Campagner, Ronzio, Cameli, Mandoli, Pastore, Sconfienza, Folgado, Barandas, Gamboa
studies.summary_of_findings: Confirmed the overall utility of AI support, but found that XAI can be associated with a 'WHITE-BOX PARADOX' — producing a null or detrimental effect on diagnostic accuracy. Separately and more provocatively, AI-FIRST protocols were associated with HIGHER diagnostic accuracy than Human-first protocols. The authors caution that AI-first protocols are not immune to specific cognitive biases, naming algorithmic aversion and conservatism bias. This is the clearest counter-evidence in the base against the widespread assumption that making people commit to a judgement before seeing the AI is protective.
studies.authors_framing: AUTHORS' WORDS: the 'white-box paradox' — explanations intended to make the model transparent produce 'a null or detrimental effect.' On protocols they report that AI-first outperforms human-first while cautioning these protocols 'are not immune to specific cognitive biases such as algorithmic aversion and conservatism bias.' MECHANISM IS BIAS-BASED, not effort-based: committing first can entrench a wrong prior (conservatism bias), while seeing the AI first can trigger rejection of correct advice (algorithmic aversion). Note this sits in direct tension with Buçinca's cognitive-forcing result, which is a real disagreement in the literature and not a coding error.
studies.design_notes: Two things varied. COLLABORATION PROTOCOL: AI-first (recommendation shown before the human decides) versus Human-first (human commits first). And XAI: presence and type, including narrative explanations and activation maps. Two user studies — 12 specialist radiologists on knee MRI (240 cases) and 44 ECG readers of VARYING EXPERTISE (20 cases), which is why expertise is coded as manipulated rather than fixed. One of only a handful of studies in this base with genuine domain experts on hard clinical material.

studies.study: Assertiveness-based Agent Communication for Personalized Medicine on Medical Imaging Diagnosis
studies.author: Calisto, Santiago, Nunes, Nascimento
studies.summary_of_findings: Tone is not cosmetic. Personalising assertiveness to each clinician's professional experience REDUCED MEDICAL ERRORS and increased satisfaction, with statistically significant differences between clinicians of different experience levels. Of the 52 participants who expressed a preference, 66% chose the assertiveness-based agent over the conventional one, 24% preferred the conventional agent and 10% had no preference. The information content was held constant throughout — only the register in which it was asserted changed.
studies.authors_framing: AUTHORS' FRAMING: 'assertiveness plays an important role in how this communication is perceived and its benefits', and personalising it 'according to the professional experience of each clinician can reduce medical errors and increase satisfaction.' MECHANISM IS SOCIAL / COMMUNICATIVE rather than cognitive: nothing about the explanation content changes, only the delivery register, and the optimal register depends on the recipient's expertise. This is the only study in the base that isolates delivery style from information content, and it suggests the AI design factor carries effects that have nothing to do with what the AI knows.
studies.design_notes: ASSERTIVENESS OF THE AGENT'S TONE is the manipulation — a suggestive (non-assertive) versus an imposing (assertive) communication style delivering IDENTICAL diagnostic content for breast cancer. The agent presented number of detected findings, cancer severity per breast and per imaging modality, a visual severity scale, its own sensitivity and specificity, and clinical arguments about pathological co-variables. Clinician EXPERIENCE LEVEL is the analysed moderator.

studies.study: Understanding the Role of Human Intuition on Reliance in Human-AI Decision-Making with Explanations
studies.author: Chen, Liao, Wortman Vaughan, Bansal
studies.summary_of_findings: Think-aloud, mixed-methods study crossing two explanation types (feature-based and example-based) with two prediction tasks. The core result is a within-study contrast: feature-based explanations did NOT improve decision outcomes and INCREASED over-reliance on the AI, while example-based explanations improved performance over feature-based and helped achieve complementary human-AI performance. Same study, same tasks, opposite directions by explanation type. The qualitative analysis identifies three types of intuition decision-makers bring to bear — intuition about the task outcome, about the features, and about AI limitations — and three pathways by which they apply that intuition to override AI predictions.
studies.authors_framing: AUTHORS' WORDS: reliance depends on 'how decision-makers reconcile their own intuition — beliefs or heuristics, based on prior knowledge, experience, or pattern recognition, used to make judgments — with the information provided by the AI system to determine when to override AI predictions.' They 'use these pathways to explain why (1) the feature-based explanations we used did not improve participants' decision outcomes and increased their overreliance on AI, and (2) the example-based explanations we used improved decision-makers' performance over feature-based explanations and helped achieve complementary human-AI performance.' The mechanism is whether the explanation format gives intuition something to act on.
studies.design_notes: XAI TYPE is the manipulation: feature-based versus example-based explanations, crossed with two prediction tasks. Think-aloud protocol with mixed-methods analysis. NOTE: task difficulty and AI accuracy are marked Not reported because they were not verified in the portion of the paper read — the abstract does not state them. Verify against the methods section before relying on those two cells.

studies.study: Are Two Heads Better Than One in AI-Assisted Decision Making? Comparing the Behavior and Performance of Groups and Individuals in Human-AI Collaborative Recidivism Risk Assessment
studies.author: Chiang, Lu, Li, Yin
studies.summary_of_findings: Compared to individuals, groups relied on the AI MORE regardless of whether the AI was correct — group deliberation did not produce better-calibrated reliance. But the picture is not simply worse: groups were MORE confident when they did overturn incorrect AI recommendations, and were more willing to give the AI credit when decisions turned out correct. Groups also made FAIRER decisions than individuals on an accuracy-equality criterion. Decision accuracy itself did not differ between groups and individuals. NOTE: task difficulty and AI accuracy marked Not reported — not verified in the portion read.
studies.authors_framing: AUTHORS' FRAMING: the group is not a neutral container for AI advice. Deliberation raises overall reliance on the AI while simultaneously raising confidence in the specific cases where the group does override — suggesting groups shift WHERE their scrutiny lands rather than how much of it there is. The authors compare along six dimensions rather than advancing one causal mechanism, so this should be treated as a descriptive contrast, not a mechanistic account. Directly relevant to the multi-agent RQ.
studies.design_notes: TEAM COMPOSITION is the manipulation: individuals versus groups making a collaborative recidivism risk assessment with AI support. The comparison runs along six dimensions — decision accuracy, decision confidence, appropriateness of reliance on AI, understanding of the AI, decision fairness, and willingness to take accountability. No explanation was provided in either condition, so this isolates the group effect from any XAI effect.

studies.study: AI Trust: Can Explainable AI Enhance Warranted Trust?
studies.author: de Brito Duarte, Correia, Arriaga, Paiva
studies.summary_of_findings: Tests the common premise that XAI explanations increase trust in AI, and shows the increase 'may depend on many factors'. Trust in an AI recommendation system was examined as a joint function of explanation presence, system performance and risk level, rather than explanation alone. CODED FROM ABSTRACT ONLY — Regina, fill in the directional results and effect sizes from your own paper. These are the one set of numbers in this base you can supply without a literature search, and this row will be stronger than any other once you do.
studies.authors_framing: AUTHORS' WORDS: 'The underlying premise is that the explanations of the XAI models enhance AI trust. However, such an increase may depend on many factors.' The mechanism proposed is CONDITIONALITY rather than a single pathway — explanation effects on trust are moderated by system performance and by risk. Sits alongside Vasconcelos 2023 as an argument that the null and positive XAI results scattered across this literature reflect unmeasured moderators rather than an unstable underlying effect.
studies.design_notes: THREE FACTORS crossed: presence of EXPLANATIONS, SYSTEM PERFORMANCE (AI accuracy), and LEVEL OF RISK. This is one of only two studies in the base that manipulates AI performance directly, and one of only two that manipulates stakes — which makes it unusually well specified for the framework's purposes. OWN WORK (MSc). Regina: fill in the directional results and effect sizes from your own paper.

studies.study: Effects of XAI on trust and human behavior in a high-risk decision task
studies.author: Leichtmann, Humer, Hinterreiter, Streit, Mara
studies.summary_of_findings: Explanations (attribution plus example-based) improved outcomes and produced better-calibrated trust than no explanation. The EDUCATIONAL intervention — telling people how the AI works in general — did NOT help. CAUTION: an earlier version of this row claimed domain knowledge and AI knowledge had no effect on performance. That claim came from the old spreadsheet and is NOT verified against the results section. Treat the education null as verified and the knowledge nulls as unverified until the full paper is read.
studies.authors_framing: AUTHORS' FRAMING treats XAI method and educational intervention as separable levers on trust and behaviour in a high-risk task. The design implies a mechanism distinction between explaining THIS DECISION (attribution and example-based, which helped) and explaining HOW THE SYSTEM WORKS in general (education, which did not). If that holds, global model understanding does not substitute for case-level explanation — which parallels Zhang 2020's finding that global accuracy figures cannot support case-level discrimination.
studies.design_notes: 2x2 BETWEEN-SUBJECTS, N=410 online — the largest sample in the base. Factor 1: XAI — attribution-based PLUS example-based explanations of the AI's predictions, versus none. Factor 2: EDUCATIONAL INTERVENTION — additional information on how the AI works, versus none. Virtual mushroom hunt: pick only edible mushrooms and avoid poisonous ones, assisted by an AI app classifying mushroom images. Stakes are simulated through poisoning consequences rather than real risk.

studies.study: Appropriate Reliance on AI Advice: Conceptualization and the Effect of Explanations
studies.author: Schemmer, Kuehl, Benz, Bartos, Satzger
studies.summary_of_findings: Conceptual and empirical paper that splits appropriate reliance into two orthogonal measures: Relative AI Reliance (RAIR) — accepting the AI's advice when the AI is right and your own initial judgement was wrong — and Relative Self-Reliance (RSR) — rejecting the AI's advice when your own answer was right and the AI's was not. Explanations had a SIGNIFICANT effect on RAIR but NO significant effect on RSR. Explanations therefore improved participants' uptake of correct AI advice without improving their resistance to incorrect advice. This is the clearest single argument in the base for never collapsing over- and under-reliance into one 'reliance' outcome.
studies.authors_framing: AUTHORS' WORDS: appropriate reliance is two-dimensional, not one. Explanations operate on the dimension of accepting good advice (RAIR) and leave untouched the dimension of rejecting bad advice (RSR). Implication: an intervention can raise measured 'reliance' and look successful while doing nothing about the failure mode — following a wrong AI — that actually matters for oversight.
studies.design_notes: XAI PRESENCE is the manipulation: explanation versus no explanation. The AI DESIGN is not incidental — a two-stage human-first protocol (participant commits to an independent judgement, then sees the AI advice) is REQUIRED to compute RAIR and RSR at all, since both measures need to know what the person thought before the AI spoke. Any study without that two-stage structure cannot separate over- from under-reliance. NOTE: difficulty and AI accuracy marked Not reported — not verified in the portion read.

studies.study: Ignore, Trust, or Negotiate: Clinician Acceptance of AI-Based Treatment Recommendations
studies.author: Sivaraman, Bukowski, Levin, Kahn, Perer
studies.summary_of_findings: Explanations generally increased confidence in the AI. But the substantive contribution is that concordance with recommendations did not fit the binary accept/reject framing used almost everywhere else in this literature. Clinicians sometimes ignored the AI and sometimes trusted it, but they OFTEN prioritised particular aspects of a recommendation to follow, reject, or delay — a process the authors call NEGOTIATION. This is a direct challenge to how reliance is operationalised across the rest of the evidence base, where agreement with the AI's final answer is the standard measure.
studies.authors_framing: AUTHORS' WORDS: the three-way categorisation 'ignore, trust, or negotiate' replaces binary acceptance. Clinicians 'often prioritized aspects of the recommendations to follow, reject, or delay in a process we term negotiation.' This is a MEASUREMENT IMPLICATION more than a causal mechanism: if real expert reliance is partial and component-wise, then binary agreement-based reliance measures are mis-specified for complex treatment decisions. Speaks directly to the CAT's own critique of reliance measurement in section 2.3.
studies.design_notes: XAI TYPE inside a purpose-built interpretable decision-support interface for sepsis treatment: text-only, feature importance, and alternative-treatment probabilities. 24 intensive care clinicians made AI-assisted decisions on REAL patient cases. Mixed-methods design.

studies.study: Explanations Can Reduce Overreliance on AI Systems During Decision-Making
studies.author: Vasconcelos, Jörke, Grunde-McLaughlin, Gerstenberg, Bernstein, Krishna
studies.summary_of_findings: Five studies, N=731, maze task with a simulated AI. In the easy and medium-difficulty conditions there was NO difference between prediction-only and explanation conditions — explanations reduced over-reliance only in the HARD task condition, where exploratory analysis also showed improved decision accuracy. Study 2 and 3 manipulated explanation difficulty; Study 4 manipulated monetary compensation for correct answers; both moved over-reliance in the direction the cost-benefit account predicts. Study 5 adapted the Cognitive Effort Discounting paradigm to quantify the utility of different explanations. The authors position this directly against the view that over-reliance is an inevitability of human cognition.
studies.authors_framing: AUTHORS' WORDS: 'people strategically choose whether or not to engage with an AI explanation.' They 'formalize this strategic choice in a cost-benefit framework, where the costs and benefits of engaging with the task are weighed against the costs and benefits of relying on the AI.' Crucially for the field: 'some of the null effects found in literature could be due in part to the explanation not sufficiently reducing the costs of verifying the AI's prediction.' Explicitly rejects the cognitive-bias / uncalibrated-trust account.
studies.design_notes: Four things varied across five studies on a maze task with a simulated AI. Study 1: TASK DIFFICULTY (easy / medium / hard) crossed with explanation presence. Studies 2-3: EXPLANATION DIFFICULTY / cognitive load, holding task constant. Study 4: STAKES — monetary compensation for correct answers, i.e. the benefit side of the ledger. Study 5: explanation utility quantified via the Cognitive Effort Discounting paradigm. The design is built to move costs and benefits independently, which is what makes it a TEST of the cost-benefit account rather than an observation of it.

studies.study: Decision control and explanations in human-AI collaboration: Improving user perceptions and compliance
studies.author: Westphal, Vössing, Satzger, Yom-Tov, Rafaeli
studies.summary_of_findings: The two levers move in OPPOSITE directions in the same study. DECISION CONTROL positively affected trust and understanding and improved compliance with system recommendations. EXPLANATION PRESENCE IMPAIRED rather than improved user outcomes. Critically, the authors identify the route: the negative effect of explanation presence was explained by INCREASES IN PERCEIVED TASK COMPLEXITY. This is the only study in the base that reports a measured mediator for an explanation harm.
studies.authors_framing: AUTHORS' WORDS, from cognitive load theory: the negative effect of explanation presence on user outcomes 'was explained by increases in perceived task complexity.' Explanations add load, and load degrades outcomes. Decision control operates by a different route entirely — granting adjustment authority raises trust and understanding directly. This is the closest INDEPENDENT corroboration of the cost side of Vasconcelos's cost-benefit account, arrived at from a different theoretical starting point and with a measured mediator rather than an inferred one.
studies.design_notes: TWO TECHNIQUES crossed, both drawn from cognitive load theory. (1) DECISION CONTROL — users empowered to ADJUST the system's recommendations rather than only accept or reject them. (2) EXPLANATION PRESENCE — explanations of the system's reasoning, or none. The explanation TYPE is not verified from the portion read, which is why only 'XAI: None' appears in the category list.

studies.study: Explanations Considered Harmful: The Impact of Misleading Explanations on Accuracy in Hybrid Human-AI Decision Making
studies.author: Cabitza, Fregosi, Campagner, Natali
studies.summary_of_findings: Introduces the 'XAI HALO EFFECT': participants were influenced by the misleading explanations to the extent that they DID NOT VERIFY the correctness of the advice, despite the advice being accurate. A bad explanation attached to good advice degrades the decision. Best Paper Award at the World Conference on Explainable AI. Directly consequential for the EU AI Act Article 14 framing: an explanation can be present, satisfy a transparency requirement, and still actively impair oversight rather than support it.
studies.authors_framing: AUTHORS' TERM: the 'XAI halo effect' — the presence and apparent coherence of an explanation substitutes for verification of the recommendation itself. Participants did not check the advice because the explanation supplied an impression of having understood. MECHANISM: explanation quality operates independently of, and can override, advice quality. This is a fifth distinct account in the base, and the only one in which the explanation causes harm through its FORM rather than through its cognitive cost or the reasoning it does or does not demand.
studies.design_notes: EXPLANATION QUALITY, holding ADVICE quality constant. Participants received ACCURATE AI advice paired with MISLEADING explanations, on logic puzzle tasks. This is the only design in the base that decouples the correctness of the recommendation from the correctness of the explanation. SCHEMA NOTE: explanation quality is orthogonal to explanation type, so it does not sit naturally in the XAI column — if more quality-manipulating studies appear, quality should get its own column.

studies.study: Never tell me the odds: Investigating pro-hoc explanations in medical decision making
studies.author: Cabitza, Natali, Famiglini, Campagner, Caccavella, Gallazzi
studies.summary_of_findings: Pro-hoc XAI aided doctors, enhancing decision-making for NOVICES without accuracy loss for others. The stated aim is to reduce over-reliance rather than merely to give advice. Withholding the AI's numerical confidence while supplying similar cases converts the support from a verdict into evidence the clinician has to weigh — there is no longer an answer available to defer to.
studies.authors_framing: AUTHORS' TERM: 'Frictional AI' — systems that deliberately embed COGNITIVE FRICTION for better decisions. Their framing: pro-hoc explanations 'aim to reduce over-reliance, not just give advice.' The mechanism is removal of the deferrable object: by withholding the odds and supplying similar cases instead, the design eliminates the thing that would otherwise be accepted wholesale. A sixth distinct account in the base, closest in spirit to Buçinca's cognitive forcing but implemented in WHAT INFORMATION IS GIVEN rather than in the interaction protocol.
studies.design_notes: PRO-HOC EXPLANATIONS: the decision support provides explanations by SIMILAR CASES while WITHHOLDING the AI's probability estimate — hence 'never tell me the odds'. 16 orthopedists assessed fracture detection. Expertise (novice versus experienced) is analysed. The authors situate this within 'Frictional AI': systems that deliberately embed cognitive friction to improve decisions.

studies.study: Does More Advice Help? The Effects of Second Opinions in AI-Assisted Decision Making
studies.author: Lu, Wang, Yin
manipulated_factors: AI design: Second opinion always shown
AI design: Second opinion on request
studies.summary_of_findings: CORRECTS THE OLD CODING, which said only that 'agreement level matters, not source'. The actual result is about CONTROL. When a second opinion is ALWAYS presented alongside the AI recommendation, decision-makers reduce over-reliance BUT INCREASE UNDER-RELIANCE — regardless of whether the second opinion came from a peer or another AI. When decision-makers instead CONTROL when to solicit a peer's second opinion, their active solicitations can mitigate over-reliance WITHOUT inducing increased under-reliance, in some cases. Adding advice is not free; who chooses when to add it is what determines whether you trade one failure mode for the other.
studies.authors_framing: AUTHORS' FRAMING: inappropriate reliance is the target, and second opinions are tested as a remedy. The mechanism that emerges is AGENCY OVER INFORMATION FLOW rather than the information itself — identical content, imposed versus requested, produces different reliance profiles. Converges with Westphal 2023 (decision control helps) and with the second-opinion structure being directly relevant to Regina's multi-agent RQ6, where multiple AI advisors are exactly the always-present condition.
studies.design_notes: SECOND OPINIONS, crossed two ways. (1) SOURCE: a peer's second opinion versus another AI model's. (2) CONTROL: whether the second opinion is ALWAYS PRESENTED alongside the AI recommendation, or SOLICITED BY THE DECISION-MAKER when they choose. Three pre-registered randomised human-subject experiments — the only pre-registered work in this base.

studies.study: Dealing with Uncertainty: Understanding the Impact of Prognostic Versus Diagnostic Tasks on Trust and Reliance in Human-AI Decision Making
studies.author: Salimzadeh, He, Gadiraju
studies.summary_of_findings: TWO RESULTS, and the second is the interesting one. First: task complexity and uncertainty significantly increase reliance on the AI — with complex and uncertain tasks, users relied MORE while showing LOWER appropriate reliance. Second and more striking: USER TRUST WAS NOT INFLUENCED by task complexity or uncertainty at all. Behaviour moved and the attitude did not. That is a clean dissociation between self-reported trust and behavioural reliance within a single study, and it is the sharpest evidence in the base that the two must not be treated as proxies for one another.
studies.authors_framing: AUTHORS' FRAMING: 'with the presence of uncertainty in a task, individuals may lack sufficient capability to verify the correctness of AI advice and therefore rely more heavily on the AI systems, leading to reduced appropriate reliance.' The mechanism is VERIFIABILITY — uncertainty removes the ability to check, not the willingness. This is a close cousin of Vasconcelos's cost account but locates the problem in the task's epistemic structure rather than in effort: on a prognostic task there is no ground truth available to verify against at any price.
studies.design_notes: TASK COMPLEXITY and TASK UNCERTAINTY, operationalised as DIAGNOSTIC versus PROGNOSTIC tasks. Diagnostic tasks have a clear ground truth; prognostic tasks require predicting future outcomes and so carry irreducible uncertainty. Between-subjects, N=258, trip-planning context.

studies.study: Accuracy-Time Tradeoffs in AI-Assisted Decision Making under Time Pressure
studies.author: UNRESOLVED
studies.design_notes: Time pressure manipulated against a no-pressure baseline, crossed with task difficulty (hard vs easy) and the timing of AI assistance (no AI, AI before the human decides, AI after, mixed). Personality was measured. This row had been blanked at some point during the session and has been fully restored here.

studies.study: Contrastive Explanations That Anticipate Human Misconceptions Can Improve Human Decision-Making Skills
studies.author: Buçinca, Swaroop, Paluch, Doshi-Velez, Gajos
studies.summary_of_findings: Large sample (N=628) and aimed directly at the deskilling question. Contrastive explanations SIGNIFICANTLY ENHANCED users' INDEPENDENT decision-making skills compared to unilateral explanations, WITHOUT sacrificing decision accuracy. The paper's opening premise is itself worth recording as a finding: 'people's decision-making abilities often fail to improve or may even erode when they rely on AI for decision-support, even when the AI provides informative explanations.' CORRECTS THE OLD CODING — the previous spreadsheet entry claimed 'learning was improved with contrastive explanations but overreliance was not improved'. Over-reliance is not the reported outcome here; independent decision-making skill is.
studies.authors_framing: AUTHORS' WORDS: 'people intuitively seek contrastive explanations, which clarify the difference between the AI's decision and their own reasoning, while most AI systems offer "unilateral" explanations that justify the AI's decision but do not account for users' thinking.' MECHANISM IS ALIGNMENT OF HUMAN AND AI KNOWLEDGE: an explanation only teaches if it addresses the gap between what the AI concluded and what the user would have concluded. Important implication for the framework — this makes the explanation's effect depend on a HUMAN-side variable (the user's likely prior judgement), not on an AI-side property alone. Seventh distinct author-proposed mechanism in the base.
studies.design_notes: EXPLANATION TYPE: human-centred CONTRASTIVE explanations — which explain the difference between the AI's choice and a PREDICTED, LIKELY HUMAN choice on the same task — versus 'unilateral' explanations that justify the AI's decision without accounting for the user's thinking. Large-scale experiment, N=628. The framework generates the contrast by first predicting what the user would probably have concluded, which makes the explanation depend on a human-side variable.

studies.study: From Oracular to Judicial: Enhancing Clinical Decision Making through Contrasting Explanations and a Novel Interaction Protocol
studies.author: Cabitza, Natali et al.
studies.summary_of_findings: Motivated explicitly by automation bias, diminished sense of agency, and over-reliance on clinical decision support systems in settings where decision-making autonomy matters. The protocol is designed to encourage engagement and critical evaluation rather than acceptance. The paper assesses whether this affects diagnostic accuracy and how. NOTE: the ACM abstract page states the design and motivation clearly but the specific directional results are not recoverable from the portion read — fetch the full text before citing effect sizes.
studies.authors_framing: AUTHORS' FRAMING: moving from an ORACULAR mode (the system pronounces a verdict) to a JUDICIAL one (the system presents competing considerations for the human to adjudicate). The mechanism is removal of the verdict combined with forced prior commitment — automation bias needs an authoritative output to attach to, and agency is preserved by making the clinician rule rather than receive a ruling. LAB CONCENTRATION NOTE: same Cabitza/Natali group as the 'white-box paradox' and 'pro-hoc / Frictional AI' rows. Three of the strongest anti-oracular findings come from one group.
studies.design_notes: 'JUDICIAL AI' — a novel interaction protocol that presents CONTRASTING EXPLANATIONS to medical professionals rather than definitive recommendations. Two design features combine: (1) the protocol ensures users form an INDEPENDENT JUDGEMENT BEFORE engaging with any AI-generated explanation, and (2) no definitive recommendation is offered at all. The baseline is the 'oracular' mode — a feature-importance style justification of a stated verdict. The independent-judgement-first structure is also what makes the influence of explanations measurable, since the user's prior position is on record.

studies.study: Is Conversational XAI All You Need? Human-AI Decision Making With a Conversational XAI Assistant
studies.author: He, Aishwarya, Gadiraju
studies.summary_of_findings: A CLEAN DISSOCIATION, and an uncomfortable one. Compared with the XAI dashboard, the conversational interface produced BETTER UNDERSTANDING of the AI system and HIGHER USER TRUST. But users of BOTH interfaces showed CLEAR OVER-RELIANCE on the AI. Improving understanding and trust did not touch the behavioural failure mode at all. This is one of the strongest arguments in the base for keeping understanding, trust and over-reliance as separate outcome columns — an intervention can move two of them favourably while leaving the third untouched.
studies.authors_framing: AUTHORS' FRAMING: the conversational interface was expected to work by increasing engagement, and it did improve subjective understanding and trust. But the paper's own result undercuts the inference chain from engagement to calibrated reliance. Reads directly against Buçinca 2020's warning that subjective measures do not predict objective performance — here is a case where subjective measures improved and behaviour did not. Directly relevant to Regina's own conversational-systems study.
studies.design_notes: XAI DELIVERY MODALITY: a conversational XAI interface versus a conventional XAI dashboard, holding the underlying explanation content constant. The premise under test is that augmenting existing XAI methods with a conversational user interface will increase engagement and boost understanding of the AI system.

studies.study: Towards Human-AI Deliberation: Design and Evaluation of LLM-Empowered Deliberative AI
studies.author: Ma, Chen, Wang, Zheng, Peng, Yin, Ma
studies.summary_of_findings: Deliberative AI outperformed traditional XAI systems by fostering APPROPRIATE reliance and improving task performance. The system is explicitly designed both to resolve human-AI conflicts and to mitigate inappropriate reliance, and it constrains the interaction according to principles drawn from deliberation theory. The authors report that following those principles in constraining interaction helps improve decision accuracy on sensitive binary tasks.
studies.authors_framing: AUTHORS' FRAMING: constraining the interaction according to DELIBERATION THEORY — eliciting the human's opinion dimension by dimension, then structuring the disagreement — is what produces appropriate reliance. The mechanism is PROCEDURAL: the AI does not present a conclusion with supporting material, it requires the human to state a position first and then negotiates over it. Converges with Gajos 2022's withheld-conclusion result and with Sivaraman 2023's observed 'negotiation', but built into the system rather than observed in clinicians.
studies.design_notes: AI INTERACTION ARCHITECTURE: Deliberative AI — dimension-level opinion elicitation, iterative decision updates, and structured discussion between human and AI, powered by an LLM interfacing with domain-specific models — versus traditional XAI. Task: graduate admission decisions, a sensitive binary task. Mixed-methods user study. NOTE: this is CHI 2025, not 2024 as previously recorded.
